subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Helminths are multicellular parasites that cause a spectrum of diseases in East Africa. Clinical reasoning focuses on exposure history, eosinophilia, and limited diagnostics, guiding empiric anthelmintic therapy and supportive care.

sections.p: Helminths are multicellular eukaryotes that infect humans through soil, water, or food. In low‑resource settings they are a major cause of morbidity, especially among children.
b: Transmit via soil, water, food, or vectors

sections.p: They are large, motile, and have complex life cycles involving intermediate hosts or environmental stages.
b: Life cycle often includes an intermediate host

t.b: Detects eggs or larvae; positive indicates active infection

sections.p: Transmission routes vary: soil‑borne (Ascaris, hookworm), water‑borne (Schistosoma), or food‑borne (Angiostrongylus).
b: Raw or undercooked snails for rat lungworm

sections.p: Helminths cause a range of clinical syndromes: intestinal obstruction, anemia, growth retardation, eosinophilic meningitis, and chronic liver disease.

t.b: >500/µL suggests helminth infection; high in eosinophilic meningitis

sections.p: History, eosinophilia, and simple stool microscopy are the cornerstones. Advanced imaging is rarely available.

t.b: Detects antibodies; positive supports diagnosis when microscopy is negative

sections.p: Empiric broad‑spectrum anthelmintics are first line. Supportive care for anemia and nutritional rehabilitation is essential.
b: Avoid praziquantel if severe hepatic dysfunction

t.b: Monitor for anemia; transfuse if <7 g/dL

sections.p: Remember that eosinophilic meningitis presents with headache, neck stiffness, and eosinophilia in CSF. In low‑resource settings, a positive history of raw snail ingestion is key.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting (possible obstruction), persistent high fever, neurological deficits, or haemorrhagic complications

faq.q: What is the most common helminth in East Africa?
faq.a: Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus) causes chronic anemia and protein loss.

faq.q: How do you differentiate Ascaris from hookworm on stool?
faq.a: Ascaris eggs are large, oval with bipolar plugs; hookworm eggs are smaller, oval, with a single polar plug.

faq.q: Why is albendazole preferred over mebendazole in schistosomiasis?
faq.a: Albendazole is effective against adult worms and has better tissue penetration; mebendazole is less effective for schistosomiasis.

exam: A 5‑year‑old boy from a rural village presents with abdominal pain and vomiting. Stool microscopy shows large, oval eggs with bipolar plugs. — Identify the parasite, explain the likely complication, and outline first‑line treatment.

A 28‑year‑old woman returns from a trip to a coastal area with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. CSF shows 15% eosinophils. — What is the most likely diagnosis, what exposure is key, and what drug is contraindicated in severe hepatic disease?
A 12‑year‑old girl has chronic cough and weight loss. Blood shows eosinophilia >800/µL. Stool microscopy is negative. — Discuss the next diagnostic step and why serology may be useful.
A patient with known hookworm infection develops severe anemia and requires transfusion. — What supportive measures should accompany anthelmintic therapy?
A 7‑year‑old child presents with intestinal obstruction. Imaging is unavailable. — What bedside sign suggests Ascaris obstruction, and what is the immediate management?
A 35‑year‑old man with chronic schistosomiasis presents with portal hypertension. — What long‑term complication should you monitor for, and what screening test is most practical?
A 4‑year‑old child has a rash and eosinophilia after eating raw snails. — Explain why this presentation is dangerous and what immediate treatment should be started.

A 60‑year‑old patient with HIV presents with abdominal pain and eosinophilia. Stool microscopy is negative. — Discuss how immunosuppression alters the presentation of helminth infections and what empiric therapy you would consider.
